questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Identify the rule applied when a court order conflicts with a statute
questions.stem: Ticket CORE-1180 asks which rule governs when a district court order grants relief that a federal statute appears to forbid.

options.text: The statute controls, because a court order cannot override what Congress enacted.
options.misconception: believes any statute outranks a final judgment

options.text: The order controls, because finality protects the losing party from further litigation.
options.misconception: treats finality as absolute and blocks appellate review

options.text: The conflict is resolved by the higher court on appeal, using ordinary error review.
The order is void until the agency that administers the statute reauthorizes it.
options.misconception: assumes agency consent is needed to enforce a judgment

questions.explanation: A conflict between an order and a statute is reviewed for legal error by the higher court. Finality does not bar correction of an erroneous legal ruling, and no agency reauthorization is required.
questions.hint: Think about the standard applied on appeal.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a court should decide a constitutional issue rather than a statutory one
questions.stem: The release review recorded a drafting question: when should a court decide a constitutional issue rather than a statutory one?

answer.exemplar: A court should resolve a constitutional question only when the case cannot be decided on statutory grounds and a party has the right to raise it. Otherwise the court reads the statute in a way that avoids the constitutional problem and decides the statutory issue, which decides less and risks less.

questions.explanation: Constitutional avoidance keeps courts on the statutory ground when a reasonable reading exists. The constitutional issue is reached only if the statute cannot avoid the conflict and a challenger may properly assert it.
questions.hint: Avoid the constitutional question if possible.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a proposed remedy stays within the authority of the court

stimulus.body: A reviewer memo notes that the trial court entered judgment for the only named plaintiff and stated that the ruling applied to the company's product line generally. Counsel replies that a court may order relief for the parties before it, and no more.

questions.stem: According to the attached memo, why is the trial court's stated reach over the whole product line problematic?

options.text: The product line is covered because the court may declare the general legal status of the parties' dispute.
options.misconception: assumes a judgment binds everyone in the industry

options.text: The problem is that no damages were awarded, so the judgment has no operative effect at all.
options.misconception: believes a judgment without damages is void

options.text: The issue is the court's lack of jurisdiction, because the company never consented to the case.
options.misconception: confuses a scope defect with a consent defect

options.text: The problem is that a court cannot grant relief to non-parties, so the stated reach exceeds what it may order.

questions.explanation: Relief is limited to the parties and the controversy before the court, so a court may not extend it to non-parties. A general declaration covering a whole product line asks the court to order more than it is authorized to award.
questions.hint: Relief follows the parties before the court.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the binding effect and enforcement of a consent decree

stimulus.body: A regulator and a company agree to settle litigation. The court enters their negotiated terms as a consent decree and retains jurisdiction to enforce it. The decree states that it is not precedent for other matters and binds only the parties.

questions.stem: A support agent asks what the consent decree described in the scenario does and does not do for the company.

options.text: It settles this dispute permanently and also serves as persuasive example for other companies.
options.misconception: treats a settlement as binding precedent on outsiders

options.text: It settles this dispute and binds only the parties, while the court keeps power to enforce it.
It permanently enjoins the company from the regulated conduct, so the agency need not sue again.
options.misconception: confuses a settlement with a permanent injunction

options.text: It ends the case but removes the court's authority to enforce the agreed terms later.
options.misconception: assumes entry as a decree ends enforcement power

questions.explanation: A consent decree binds only the parties and leaves the court able to enforce it. It creates no precedent for others and does not permanently enjoin the company or bar the agency from acting elsewhere.
questions.hint: Read the decree as a settlement, not a ruling.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the review an intermediate appellate court performs
questions.stem: Two engineers dispute the outcome of a review: first, whether a court of appeals may reverse a factual finding; second, which standard applies.

options.text: First, yes; second, the reviewing court substitutes its own view of the facts under a de novo standard.
options.misconception: applies de novo review to factual findings

options.text: First, no; second, the reviewing court reviews every finding de novo because the record is cold.
options.misconception: believes all appellate review is de novo

options.text: First, yes; second, the reviewing court must assume the trial court's facts are correct always.
options.misconception: inverts the roles of reviewing and reviewing body

options.text: First, no; second, factual findings are reviewed for clear error, while legal conclusions get de novo review.

questions.explanation: Appellate courts do not reweigh the evidence and cannot substitute their judgment for the fact-finder's. Factual findings are reversed only if clearly erroneous, while legal conclusions are reviewed independently.
questions.hint: Facts and law get different appellate treatment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the limits on when a writ of mandamus is available
questions.stem: When a service tier is retired, the team asks whether a court may order a public officer to perform a task that the law leaves to discretion.

options.text: Yes, because mandamus lies whenever a party shows an unreasonable delay by an officer.
options.misconception: confuses unreasonable delay with any ministerial duty

options.text: Yes, because mandamus is available once the officer has already refused to decide the matter.
options.misconception: assumes a refusal always makes the duty ministerial

options.text: No, because mandamus reaches only ministerial duties that the law leaves no discretion to decide.
No, because a court may never order any officer to act in an individual case.
options.misconception: overstates the bar and treats mandamus as unavailable

questions.explanation: A writ of mandamus compels performance of a ministerial, nondiscretionary duty. When the governing law leaves the officer latitude, the task is discretionary and cannot be compelled by that writ.
questions.hint: Ask whether the law leaves the officer any choice.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a federal habeas petition reaches and what it leaves alone
questions.stem: Most new hires ask the same thing: what does a federal habeas petition actually reach, and what does it leave alone.

answer.exemplar: Habeas corpus addresses the fact and legality of a person's custody. It can lead to release, a new trial, or a new hearing, but it does not award money damages for wrongful conviction and it does not supply a civil remedy for other harms. It reaches both federal and state custody, subject to the exhaustion requirement.

questions.explanation: Habeas is a collateral attack on custody rather than a retrial, and its remedies are release or a fresh hearing. It is not a damages remedy, and it reaches state as well as federal custody once exhaustion is satisfied.
questions.hint: Habeas is about custody, not money.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the standard governing summary judgment on the papers

stimulus.body: A memo to the review team states that the court may enter judgment without a trial when the papers show no genuine dispute of material fact, and that the court must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the party against whom judgment is sought.

questions.stem: The team asks what the memo requires before the court may decide the case on the papers.

options.text: That the moving party's evidence be stronger than the opposing party's evidence.
options.misconception: treats the motion as a weighing contest

options.text: That no genuine dispute of material fact appears, viewed in the non-moving party's favor.
That the judge personally believe the movant's account of the facts is more likely.
options.misconception: lets belief substitute for the legal test

options.text: That both sides file identical papers, since only agreement avoids a genuine dispute.
options.misconception: invents an identity requirement for the papers

questions.explanation: Summary judgment requires no genuine dispute of material fact, viewed in the light most favorable to the non-moving party. A judge's belief about which side is more likely is not the test, and identity of filings is irrelevant.
questions.hint: Doubt on the papers goes to the party resisting judgment.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Identify which authority must be resolved before a regulation may be enforced

stimulus.body: A regulation issued by a federal agency adds a reporting duty that a federal statute does not require. A company sues, and a court orders the agency to follow the regulation without passing on whether the statute permits the duty.

questions.stem: The compliance desk asks what the court should have done before issuing that order.

options.text: It should have entered judgment for the company at once, because the regulation exceeded the statute.
options.misconception: assumes the outcome is predetermined

options.text: It should have upheld the order, because a court may never question an agency's regulation.
options.misconception: treats agency rules as unreviewable

options.text: It should have decided the statutory question first, because the agency's authority depends on the statute.
It should have sent the case back to the agency, because only the agency can construe its own rule.
options.misconception: sends statutory questions back to the agency

questions.explanation: The agency's power to impose the duty comes from the statute, so that question had to be settled before the regulation could be sustained. A court cannot skip that step and enforce the duty anyway.
questions.hint: Agency power is borrowed from the statute.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Sequence statutory and constitutional questions as a court must
questions.stem: A pull request is blocked because the legal sign-off cannot tell whether to check the statute or the constitution first.

options.text: First, the constitution; second, the constitution always outranks any statutory reading.
options.misconception: makes constitutional priority automatic

options.text: First, the statute; second, a constitutional issue must still be decided even if the statute resolves the case.
options.misconception: insists constitutional questions always be reached

options.text: First, whichever the reviewing court prefers; second, preference decides the order of decision.
options.misconception: leaves priority to informal preference

options.text: First, the statute if it can resolve the case; second, the constitution only if it must be reached.

questions.explanation: The court decides the case on the statute when a reasonable construction exists and reaches the constitutional issue only if it must. Constitutional priority is about order among issues actually presented.
questions.hint: Order of decision follows necessity, not hierarchy of labels.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select the remedy a court may award on a proven loss
questions.stem: Given the new contract clause, the team asks which remedy a court may award when the proven harm is a documented lost payment.

options.text: An injunction against the payer's future payments, because damages are inadequate by definition.
options.misconception: assumes damages are never adequate

options.text: Relief confined to the loss the record supports, such as the unpaid amount plus permitted interest.
A declaration that the payer's entire business model is unlawful, to prevent future disputes.
options.misconception: expands relief beyond the claim presented

options.text: Nothing, because courts cannot award money unless the statute expressly authorizes it.
options.misconception: requires express statutory authority for damages

questions.explanation: Relief follows the claim and the proof, so a court may award the amount the record establishes along with permitted interest. It may not enjoin future payments the record does not address or declare broader unlawfulness.
questions.hint: Let the record set the size of the award.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a consent decree creates no rule of law for others
questions.stem: After a failed audit, the team asks why the settled dispute in front of them is not treated as a ruling on the law.

answer.exemplar: Because it is a consent decree: the parties negotiated the outcome and the court approved and entered it as a judgment. It resolves the claims between those parties, but a negotiated settlement is not an adjudication of what the law requires, and it establishes no rule for anyone else.

questions.explanation: A consent decree is an approved settlement, so it binds the parties and states no holding on the law. Courts do scrutinize the terms before entering them, but approval does not convert the result into precedent.
questions.hint: A negotiated outcome is not an adjudication.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Identify the scope of an intermediate appellate court's review

stimulus.body: A handbook page states that a court of appeals reviews the record made in the trial court, decides legal questions independently, and reviews factual findings only for clear error. It adds that the appellate court does not take new evidence.

questions.stem: The onboarding checklist asks which claims about appellate review the excerpt supports.

options.text: The appellate court may hold a second trial when it doubts the trial court's findings.
options.misconception: confuses review with a second trial

options.text: The appellate court may take new evidence when the record is thin on a disputed fact.
options.misconception: grants appellate courts a new evidence power

options.text: The appellate court reviews legal questions independently and checks findings only for clear error.
The appellate court must affirm whenever the trial court was not reversed at trial.
options.misconception: assumes a failure to reverse is itself an outcome

questions.explanation: Appellate courts work from the record, review legal conclusions independently, and review factual findings only for clear error. They neither retry the facts nor take new evidence, and they act on the record before them.
questions.hint: Match each claim to the record-based review the excerpt describes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the ministerial-duty test to a claimed writ

stimulus.body: A rule directs a records officer to transmit an application file to the reviewing panel on the first working day after it is complete. The officer has held the file for two months, and a lawyer asks a court to order its transmission.

questions.stem: The duty in the scenario is described as fixed, so what does that imply about the writ the lawyer seeks?

options.text: The duty looks ministerial, so the writ may lie if no other adequate remedy is available.
The duty looks discretionary, so the writ may lie because the officer took too long.
options.misconception: treats delay as proof of discretion

options.text: The duty is ministerial, so the court must issue the writ without considering other remedies.
options.misconception: assumes the writ is automatic for ministerial duties

options.text: The duty is discretionary, so the court may order transmission as a matter of equity.
options.misconception: lets equity order discretionary action

questions.explanation: A duty fixed by rule, with no discretion left to the officer, is ministerial and may be compelled if no other adequate remedy exists. The length of the delay is not what makes the duty ministerial.
questions.hint: A fixed duty points toward a ministerial claim.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the threshold and remedy for federal habeas review
questions.stem: Before the rollout, counsel asks the team to state two things about a federal habeas petition: the threshold and the remedy.

options.text: Threshold: a sentence longer than one year; remedy: money damages for the years confined.
options.misconception: keeps the one-year rule and the damages remedy

options.text: Threshold: a jury trial; remedy: a new sentence only, with no option of release.
options.misconception: invents a jury-trial threshold and limits release

options.text: Threshold: exhaustion of state remedies; remedy: release only, with no option of a new hearing.
options.misconception: limits the remedy to release alone

options.text: Threshold: custody plus exhaustion of state remedies; remedy: release, a new trial, or a new hearing.

questions.explanation: A federal habeas petition requires custody and exhaustion of available state remedies. If it succeeds, the usual remedy is release, a new trial, or a new hearing, and money damages are not available.
questions.hint: Custody, exhaustion, and non-monetary remedies.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the benefit the non-moving party receives on summary judgment
questions.stem: Because the deadline moved, the team asks what the non-moving party gains from the standard governing summary judgment.

options.text: It gains a hearing, because the motion always leads to a trial on the papers alone.
options.misconception: assumes a trial follows the motion

options.text: It gains the benefit of the doubt, since the evidence is read in its favor on a genuine dispute.
It gains nothing, because the moving party's showing alone decides the motion.
options.misconception: ignores the non-movant's evidentiary showing

options.text: It gains a burden shift, because it must prove that no dispute exists.
options.misconception: puts the summary judgment burden on the non-movant

questions.explanation: The non-moving party benefits from the rule that the evidence is viewed in its favor, and it need only show that a genuine dispute exists to defeat the motion. The burden of proving no dispute stays with the movant.
questions.hint: Doubt on the papers runs against the mover.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a court should do when its intended order conflicts with a statute
questions.stem: The quarterly review asks what a trial court should do when a party shows that the order it is about to enter conflicts with a statute.

answer.exemplar: The court should address the conflict directly and conform its order to the governing statute, because a court may not grant relief the legislature withheld. If the conflict makes the requested relief unlawful, the court should say so and give judgment for the party entitled to it, rather than entering an order the law does not support.

questions.explanation: A court may not grant relief a statute forbids, so the trial court must confront the conflict and conform its order to the law. The alternative of entering the order anyway simply creates an error for review.
questions.hint: Conform the order to the statute before entering it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose between statutory and constitutional readings that avoid a constitutional conflict

stimulus.body: A review memorandum notes that the statute can be read either to cover the disputed records or to exempt them, and that the constitutional objection to the broader reading would be severe if it were the correct one.

questions.stem: The memorandum asks which reading the court should adopt on the facts it describes.

options.text: The broad reading, because a court must test doubtful statutes against the constitution at once.
options.misconception: jumps to the constitutional test early

options.text: The broad reading, because uncertainty in a statute should always be resolved in favour of coverage.
options.misconception: assumes ambiguity always favours inclusion

options.text: The narrower reading if it avoids the constitutional problem, because the court need not reach the constitution.
The narrow reading, because a statute must always be construed as narrowly as the text allows.
options.misconception: makes narrow construction an absolute rule

questions.explanation: Where a reasonable narrower reading exists, a court adopts it and decides the case on the statute, leaving the constitutional question undecided. It must reach the constitution only when the statute cannot avoid the problem.
questions.hint: Prefer the reading that avoids the constitutional fight.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether an order overreaches by reaching beyond the party that sued

stimulus.body: A restaurant sues its landlord after a flood. The court orders the landlord to pay the documented cost of repairs to the restaurant's kitchen and to take no further action regarding any other tenant's premises.

questions.stem: The landlord's counsel asks whether the order in the scenario overreaches in any respect.

options.text: No, because the relief is confined to the party that brought the claim and the loss it proved.
No, because the court may always repair the parties' business by ordering whatever seems fair.
options.misconception: describes equity as a licence to order anything

options.text: Yes, because the court had no power to order payment at all without a jury's verdict.
options.misconception: requires a jury verdict for equitable relief

options.text: Yes, because a court may never include interest or costs in a money judgment.
options.misconception: barred from awarding interest and costs

questions.explanation: The order is confined to the plaintiff and the loss that party proved, which is what a court may award. Fairness alone does not enlarge the court's authority, and money relief does not require a jury verdict.
questions.hint: Check who benefited and what the record showed.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the effect of a consent decree and how it is enforced
questions.stem: Two engineers dispute the effect of a settlement: first, what it decides; second, whether the court can still enforce it later.

options.text: First, it decides nothing; second, the court enforces it as if it were an ordinary contract claim.
options.misconception: treats the decree as a contract action

options.text: First, it resolves the claims in the action; second, the court may enforce it, including by contempt.
First, it resolves the claims and bars every other claim between the parties; second, it cannot be enforced.
options.misconception: assumes both a broad bar and no enforcement

options.text: First, it resolves nothing beyond payment; second, the court must sue the party to enforce it.
options.misconception: turns enforcement into a separate suit

questions.explanation: Entering the negotiated terms as a decree resolves the claims in the action and leaves the court able to enforce its judgment, contempt being the standard tool. Enforcement is not a separate contract lawsuit.
questions.hint: Entered as a judgment, a decree is the court's own order.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Describe the disposition options of an intermediate appellate court
questions.stem: Among several options, the guidance states the role of the intermediate appellate tier in a case that began before a single judge.

options.text: It decides the case finally, because a further appeal lies only as a matter of discretion.
options.misconception: assumes further review is effectively unavailable

options.text: It retries the case, because appellate review means holding the trial again in the same court.
options.misconception: confuses review with a second trial

options.text: It reviews the record for legal error and may affirm, reverse, or send the case back for more proceedings.
It conducts a fresh investigation, because it may hear new evidence on the appeal.
options.misconception: assumes appellate courts take new evidence

questions.explanation: A court of appeals works from the record made below. Its task is to correct legal error and, where necessary, to vacate the judgment and remand for further proceedings rather than retry the case itself.
questions.hint: Recall what an appellate court is permitted to do.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: List the elements a petition for mandamus must establish
questions.stem: Since the last release, the team asks the legal channel to explain what a petition for a writ of mandamus must show.

answer.exemplar: The petitioner must show a clear and undeniable right to the act demanded, that the duty is ministerial rather than discretionary, and that no other adequate remedy is available. The writ is extraordinary, issues only in unusual situations, and cannot be used to control the exercise of discretion or to substitute for an appeal.

questions.explanation: The writ is narrow and extraordinary, so a petitioner must satisfy each element: a ministerial duty, a clear and undeniable right, and no adequate alternative remedy. Speed or frustration alone does not meet the test.
questions.hint: Three elements: duty, right, and no alternative remedy.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the threshold requirements of a federal habeas petition

stimulus.body: A note to new paralegals states that a federal habeas petition challenges the fact or legality of a person's custody, that the petitioner must first seek relief through available state remedies, and that the writ is not a route to money damages for wrongful conviction.

questions.stem: The note tells the paralegals which of the following statements about the writ is accurate.

options.text: A petitioner may skip state remedies if the delay would exceed one year in total.
options.misconception: invents a one-year bypass of exhaustion

options.text: A petitioner must exhaust state remedies, and the writ reaches custody rather than damages.
A petitioner may obtain damages by adding a civil claim to the petition for release.
options.misconception: allows damages to ride along with the writ

options.text: A petitioner need not be in custody, because the court may review any past conviction.
options.misconception: drops the custody requirement from the writ

questions.explanation: The writ is a challenge to custody, and a federal petitioner must first seek relief through available state remedies. Delay alone does not excuse exhaustion, and money damages for wrongful conviction are not available.
questions.hint: Check the note against the two threshold conditions.

questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a summary judgment ruling can stand on disputed facts

stimulus.body: A defendant's motion for summary judgment is granted after the court reads the affidavits. The plaintiff had submitted a declaration stating that the supervisor made the disputed statement in the plaintiff's hearing. The motion was decided without a hearing on credibility.

questions.stem: The plaintiff asks whether the ruling in the scenario can stand.

options.text: No, because a genuine dispute existed on a fact the court had to credit in the plaintiff's favor.
No, because a motion for summary judgment may never be decided without oral argument.
options.misconception: invents a mandatory hearing for the motion

options.text: Yes, because declarations are weaker evidence than testimony given at trial.
options.misconception: ranks declarations below trial evidence generally

options.text: Yes, because the court may resolve credibility questions when the record is short.
options.misconception: allows credibility findings on the papers

questions.explanation: The declaration created a genuine dispute about a fact the court had to credit in the plaintiff's favor, so the motion should have been denied. Courts may not weigh credibility on affidavits and declarations.
questions.hint: Credibility disputes belong to the fact-finder.

questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: State which authority governs when an order and a statute conflict
questions.stem: Although the guideline seems clear, the team asks two questions: first, which source governs; second, what happens to a conflicting order.

options.text: First, the order governs; second, it stands because it was entered by a judge.
options.misconception: treats any judicial order as conclusive

options.text: First, the statute governs; second, the order is void and the case must be dismissed.
options.misconception: makes non-compliance end the case

options.text: First, the statute governs; second, the conflicting order is reviewed as error and may be reversed.
First, the statute and order govern equally; second, the conflict is resolved by whoever filed last.
options.misconception: makes filing order decide legal priority

questions.explanation: The statute sets the parties' rights, and a lower order that departs from it is reviewed for legal error and may be reversed. The judgment's own issuance does not make it correct or end the case.
questions.hint: Statute first, then ordinary review of the order.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the rule of avoiding a constitutional problem
questions.stem: One incident report asks the legal question of what a court must do when a statute is open to two readings and one reading avoids a constitutional problem.

options.text: It should adopt the reading that avoids the constitutional problem, if that reading is reasonable.
It should adopt the broad reading and let the challenge decide whether the problem exists.
options.misconception: reaches the constitution before trying the statute

options.text: It should declare the statute ambiguous and stop, because ambiguity ends the court's task.
options.misconception: treats ambiguity as a reason to decide nothing

options.text: It should apply the reading the agency prefers, since the agency administers the statute.
options.misconception: defers automatically to the administering agency

questions.explanation: A court adopts a reasonable construction that avoids the constitutional problem and decides the case on the statute. It reaches the constitutional question only if the statute cannot avoid it, and deference is not automatic.
questions.hint: Pick the reasonable reading that avoids the conflict.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court cannot order relief merely because it seems fair
questions.stem: The legal team asks the agent to explain why a court may not simply order whatever relief it considers fair in a dispute between two companies.

answer.exemplar: Because the court's authority to order relief comes from the claims and the governing law, not from a free-floating sense of fairness. A court may grant only relief that is warranted by the proof and supported by the record, and equitable remedies remain subject to the traditional factors. Ordering more than the case supports exceeds the court's power.

questions.explanation: Remedy must be warranted by the claims and supported by the record, and equitable relief remains subject to the traditional factors. A court's sense of fairness cannot enlarge the relief it is authorized to order.
questions.hint: Authority to award comes from the case, not from taste.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the binding effect of a consent decree entered as a judgment

stimulus.body: An order approving a settlement states that it is entered by consent, that it binds the parties and their successors in interest, that it is not a ruling on the merits or precedent for any other matter, and that the court retains jurisdiction to enforce it.

questions.stem: The order quoted above supports which statement about the settlement it approved.

options.text: It binds every company in the industry, because the entry says the terms are reasonable.
options.misconception: infers industry-wide effect from reasonableness

options.text: It binds only the parties, establishes no precedent, and remains enforceable by the court.
It is a ruling on the merits, so a later court must follow its reading of the law.
options.misconception: treats a consent decree as a precedential ruling

options.text: It ends the court's authority, because the entry of consent transfers jurisdiction away.
options.misconception: assumes entry ends the court's jurisdiction

questions.explanation: A consent decree binds the parties and their successors in interest, creates no precedent, and leaves the court with jurisdiction to enforce it. None of that makes it a ruling on the merits.
questions.hint: Read the entry language clause by clause.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Apply the law of the case on remand

stimulus.body: A court of appeals vacates the judgment of a trial court after finding that the trial court misread a statute, and the case is returned. On remand, the trial court reaches the same result, pointing to a different reading of a procedural rule that the appellate court had not addressed.

questions.stem: The trial judge's choice is most likely to be treated how on the second appeal.

options.text: Reversed, because the appellate court's earlier decision governs the trial court on every issue.
options.misconception: makes the first appeal binding on all later issues

options.text: Reversed, because the appellate court must reach the same result whenever it reverses once.
options.misconception: confuses appellate history with finality of results

options.text: Affirmed, because a trial court may take any view on a remand it was given.
options.misconception: gives the trial court free rein on remand

options.text: Reviewed for legal error, because the law of the case binds only the issues the appellate court decided.

questions.explanation: On remand the trial court must follow the appellate court's rulings on the issues actually decided, but it may decide issues the appellate court left open. The second appeal reviews that work for legal error.
questions.hint: The law of the case covers decided issues only.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify which duties and who the writ of mandamus reaches
questions.stem: While planning the migration, the team asks two things about the writ: which duties it reaches, and who may seek it.

options.text: It reaches discretionary duties, and any member of the public may seek it.
options.misconception: confuses discretion with the reach of the writ

options.text: It reaches ministerial duties, and only a party with a personal right may seek it.
options.misconception: treats a personal right alone as enough to seek the writ

options.text: It reaches ministerial duties, and the petitioner must show a clear and undeniable right.
options.misconception: omits the requirement of a clear and undeniable right

options.text: It reaches ministerial duties, and a group may seek it if the issue is of public importance.
options.misconception: invents a public importance exception

questions.explanation: The writ compels ministerial duties, and the petitioner must show a clear and undeniable right to the act demanded, along with the absence of another adequate remedy. Public importance is not a substitute for that showing.
questions.hint: Reach and standing each have their own requirement.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the threshold conditions for federal habeas review
questions.stem: An on-call engineer asks what a federal habeas court must decide before it will consider a request from a prisoner.

options.text: Whether the petitioner is in custody and has exhausted available state remedies.
Whether the petitioner has been convicted by a jury rather than by a negotiated plea.
options.misconception: invents a jury-trial requirement for habeas

options.text: Whether the sentence exceeds one year, because shorter terms fall outside the writ.
options.misconception: repeats the myth of a one-year threshold

options.text: Whether the state has declined to appeal, since a pending appeal blocks review.
options.misconception: requires the absence of a state appeal

questions.explanation: Custody and exhaustion of available state remedies are the threshold conditions. Jury trial, sentence length, and the absence of a state appeal are not gating conditions, though each is sometimes treated as one.
questions.hint: Two conditions, not a list of extra formalities.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a dispute is genuine enough to defeat summary judgment
questions.stem: Behind the feature request, the legal question is what makes a dispute genuine enough to defeat a summary judgment motion.

answer.exemplar: A dispute is genuine when the evidence, viewed in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, would permit a reasonable person to return a verdict for that party. The inquiry is not whether the court believes that party's account, nor whether the facts are crisply disputed. Credibility, weighing of evidence, and drawing inferences belong to the fact-finder.

questions.explanation: The test asks whether a reasonable person could return a verdict for the non-moving party on the evidence viewed in that party's favor. Whether the court believes the account is irrelevant, and credibility is not for the papers.
questions.hint: Ask what a reasonable person could find for the opponent.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of an order that conflicts with the governing statute

stimulus.body: An appellate opinion states that the trial court's order was entered in direct conflict with the statute the court itself construed, that the conflict is a legal error, and that the judgment must be vacated and the matter remanded for further proceedings consistent with the statute.

questions.stem: The opinion quoted above treats the conflict between the order and the statute as what.

options.text: A matter for the agency that administers the statute, which must be asked to concur.
options.misconception: requires agency concurrence before the court acts

options.text: A matter of finality, which bars any correction because the judgment was entered.
options.misconception: treats entry of judgment as immunity

options.text: An error of law that the reviewing court corrects by vacating the judgment and remanding.
A matter of legislative intent, which the court cannot consider without a new statute.
options.misconception: makes statutory change the only route to correction

questions.explanation: An order that departs from the statute the court construed is an error of law, and the reviewing court corrects it by vacating the judgment and remanding. Neither finality nor agency concurrence blocks that step.
questions.hint: A conflict is an error of law, not a jurisdictional bar.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Decide how a court should sequence statutory and constitutional questions

stimulus.body: A company challenges a state statute on federal constitutional grounds and also argues that the statute, read narrowly, does not reach its conduct. The court notes that the company's own conduct falls outside the statute on any reasonable reading, so the statutory argument resolves the case.

questions.stem: The court in the scenario should most likely proceed how.

options.text: To the constitutional question first, because a constitutional challenge is always the more urgent one.
options.misconception: makes constitutional issues automatically first

options.text: To the constitutional question first, because the statute cannot be construed narrowly for one party.
options.misconception: assumes a party controls the reading of the statute

options.text: To both questions at once, because efficiency requires deciding them together.
options.misconception: invents a rule of efficiency over sequencing

options.text: To the statutory question only, because it disposes of the case and no constitutional issue remains.

questions.explanation: Where a reasonable construction of the statute resolves the case, the court decides the statutory question and leaves the constitutional objection undecided. Deciding the constitutional issue first would decide more than the case requires.
questions.hint: A dispositive statutory reading ends the case.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the reach and basis of a court-ordered remedy
questions.stem: Noting the mixed rulings, the team asks two things about a remedy: who it must reach, and what it must be based on.

options.text: It must reach everyone affected in the market; it must be based on what the judge considers fair.
options.misconception: makes fairness the measure of market-wide relief

options.text: It must reach the parties before the court; it must be based on the claims and the proof.
It must reach the parties before the court; it must be based on whatever remedy they request.
options.misconception: assumes the parties' request defines the remedy

options.text: It must reach the regulator as well; it must be based on the agency's enforcement priorities.
options.misconception: invites courts to follow enforcement priorities

questions.explanation: Relief runs against the parties to the judgment and must be supported by the claims and the proof. It cannot reach non-parties, and it is not defined by fairness, by the relief requested, or by an agency's priorities.
questions.hint: Parties and proof, nothing else, set the remedy.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the precedential effect of negotiated terms entered as a decree
questions.stem: Because the deadline moved, the team asks what a consent decree does about the precedential effect of the terms the parties negotiated.

options.text: Nothing for outsiders, because the decree binds the parties and does not establish a rule of law.
A great deal, because a court must follow its own settlement terms in later cases.
options.misconception: treats a settlement as binding precedent

options.text: Nothing at all, because the court never approves the legal terms in a settlement.
options.misconception: assumes courts do not review settlement terms

options.text: A moderate amount, because the terms are persuasive for other parties in similar cases.
options.misconception: converts a settlement into persuasive authority

questions.explanation: A consent decree binds the parties and creates no rule of law for anyone else, and the terms are not even persuasive authority for others. Courts do approve settlement terms before entering them as judgments.
questions.hint: Approval is not adjudication, and adjudication is not precedent here.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an appellate court does when the legal reasoning is wrong but the findings stand
questions.stem: Once the appeal is filed, the team asks what happens if the appellate court concludes the trial court's legal reasoning was wrong but its findings were not.

answer.exemplar: The appellate court reverses the legal error and remands for further proceedings, because the judgment was reached by the wrong legal route. It does not disturb the findings, since those were not shown to be clearly erroneous, and it does not enter its own judgment on the facts, because it cannot find facts itself.

questions.explanation: A legal error requires the appellate court to reverse and remand even where the findings stand, because the judgment rests on the wrong route. The findings are left undisturbed and the court may not find facts itself.
questions.hint: Reverse the law, leave the facts, remand the case.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conditions governing availability of the writ of mandamus

stimulus.body: A digest of appellate decisions states that a writ of mandamus is available only where the duty to be performed is ministerial and free from discretion, the petitioner's right to the act is clear and undeniable, and no other adequate remedy exists.

questions.stem: The digest supports which statement about the availability of the writ.

options.text: The writ cannot be used to compel an official to exercise discretion, however clear the petitioner's preference.
The writ is available whenever the official's delay is unreasonable, even if the duty is discretionary.
options.misconception: treats delay as sufficient for the writ

options.text: The writ may be used to supervise an agency's decision while that decision remains pending.
options.misconception: lets the writ supervise pending decisions

options.text: The writ is unavailable whenever the petitioner could instead file an ordinary appeal.
options.misconception: ignores the other-adequate-remedy condition

questions.explanation: The three conditions mean the writ cannot reach a discretionary decision, however strong the petitioner's preference. Neither delay nor pending agency review supplies the missing elements, and the other-remedy limit is central.
questions.hint: Discretion is the first thing the writ cannot touch.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the limits on federal review of pretrial detention

stimulus.body: A pretrial detainee asks a federal court for the writ of habeas corpus to obtain a hearing on whether his detention is justified. No criminal conviction has been entered, and the state courts have not yet ruled on the detention request.

questions.stem: The federal court's response in the scenario should be based on which point.

options.text: The detention is likely unlawful, so the court should release him without a hearing.
options.misconception: releases on likelihood rather than the governing rules

options.text: The writ reaches pretrial detention, so the court should order the hearing the detainee wants.
options.misconception: ignores the limits on pretrial habeas review

options.text: The issue is moot, because no conviction exists to challenge.
options.misconception: treats the absence of conviction as mootness

options.text: Pretrial habeas review is limited and the detention remedy must be pursued in state court first.

questions.explanation: Pretrial habeas review is narrow, and a detainee generally must seek relief through the state process first. The court does not order release merely because the detention appears unlawful, and the matter is not moot.
questions.hint: Pretrial review is narrow, and exhaustion still applies.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State who must move for summary judgment and what the court must find
questions.stem: Inside the platform group, a recurring question has two parts: who must move, and what must the court see.

options.text: The party with the stronger evidence must move; the court must see a preponderance of the evidence.
options.misconception: reverses the burdens and sets a preponderance test

options.text: The party without the burden of proof must move; the court must see no genuine dispute of material fact.
Either party may move; the court must see only that the issue is important enough to decide.
options.misconception: reduces the standard to the importance of the issue

options.text: The judge may move on its own; the court must see that the trial would be unfair.
options.misconception: invents a fairness standard for judgment

questions.explanation: The party who would bear the burden of proof at trial typically moves for summary judgment, and the court must find no genuine dispute of material fact. Importance and unfairness are not the test.
questions.hint: Burden of proof points the other way.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Identify which authority controls when an order and a statute cannot both be obeyed
questions.stem: An archived ticket from last year asks which source controls when a trial court order and the statute it construed cannot both be obeyed.

options.text: The order, because it was entered by a court with authority to decide the parties' rights.
options.misconception: assumes judicial authority outranks the statute

options.text: The statute, because only the legislature may change the law after a court has construed it.
options.misconception: makes statutes immune to court construction

options.text: Neither, because the conflict must be referred to the agency that administers the statute.
options.misconception: sends judicial conflicts to the agency

options.text: The statute, and the conflicting order is reviewed as error and corrected on appeal.

questions.explanation: When the two cannot both be obeyed, the statute governs the parties' rights and the conflicting order is treated as a legal error for correction on appeal. Judicial authority does not outrank the legislature.
questions.hint: One source must yield, and the reviewer decides.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the treatment of a constitutional objection to a construed statute
questions.stem: The quarterly review asks the team to explain how a court should treat a constitutional objection to a statute it has already construed.

answer.exemplar: If the court already construed the statute and that construction avoids the constitutional problem, the constitutional objection fails on the ground of the court's own construction and need not be decided. If no reasonable construction avoids the conflict, the court must decide the constitutional question and say whether the statute is valid.

questions.explanation: A constitutional objection to a statute the court has already construed narrowly may fail because of that construction, in which case the court need not reach the constitutional question. Otherwise the court must decide it.
questions.hint: Start with the construction the court already made.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the limits on remedies to a case's pleaded claims

stimulus.body: A memorandum of law states that the remedy in a case is limited by the claims actually pleaded, that a court may not award relief for a claim that was never brought, and that relief granted to a party must be supported by the record.

questions.stem: According to the memorandum, which statement about the remedies in a case is accurate.

options.text: A court may award relief only for claims that were brought and only where the record supports it.
A court may award relief for any claim that would have been viable if it had been pleaded.
options.misconception: allows relief on unpleaded claims

options.text: A court may award relief against a party who was never joined because the claim is similar.
options.misconception: permits binding a party who was never joined

options.text: A court must award every remedy that fits the facts, even if the claim was never pleaded.
options.misconception: requires every fitting remedy regardless of pleading

questions.explanation: Remedy is limited by the claims brought and the record made. Unpleaded claims cannot be awarded, parties never joined are not bound, and the court does not add remedies the case never asked for.
questions.hint: Pleadings and record are the two limits.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a court may modify or dissolve a consent decree

stimulus.body: Years after a consent decree resolved a dispute, a party seeks to end the decree early because the conditions that justified its terms have changed. The party asks the same court that entered it for an order releasing the obligations.

questions.stem: The scenario turns on what power the court retains over a consent decree it entered.

options.text: None, because the decree became final the moment it was entered as a judgment.
options.misconception: treats entry as the end of all court power

options.text: It retains power to modify or dissolve the decree when changed circumstances make continued enforcement inequitable.
Power to award damages for the years the decree was in force, since it was a contract in effect.
options.misconception: treats the decree as a source of damages

options.text: Power only to enforce the original terms as written, with no power to end them early.
options.misconception: denies the power to modify or dissolve

questions.explanation: A court retains equitable power to modify or dissolve a consent decree when changed circumstances would make continued enforcement inequitable. Entry as a judgment does not strip that power, and damages are not the remedy.
questions.hint: Equity lets a court revisit its own consent order.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Role of the intermediate appellate tier
questions.learningObjective: Describe what an intermediate appellate court reviews and how its decisions may be reviewed further
questions.stem: Per the governance memo, the team asks two things: what the intermediate appellate tier reviews, and how its decision is treated above it.

options.text: It reviews only the record for clear error, and its decision is final unless the highest court takes it.
options.misconception: misstates its review and treats the outcome as final

options.text: It reviews legal conclusions independently, and its decision is binding on all other courts forever.
options.misconception: treats its rulings as binding on every court

options.text: It reviews legal conclusions independently, and its decisions may be reviewed further by a higher court.
It reviews nothing at all, and its decisions are merely advisory to the parties.
options.misconception: makes appellate decisions merely advisory

questions.explanation: An intermediate appellate court reviews legal conclusions independently and factual findings for clear error, and further review may lie above it. Its decisions bind the parties but are not the last word on the law.
questions.hint: It is a tier in a hierarchy, not the final word.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the elements that make a writ of mandamus available
questions.stem: The legal team asks which statement about a writ of mandamus is consistent with its narrow use.

options.text: The writ is issued whenever a party shows that a government decision is legally wrong.
options.misconception: conflates error review with the writ

options.text: The writ is issued whenever an official has refused to decide a matter within a year.
options.misconception: makes a delay of one year the trigger

options.text: The writ is issued whenever no other remedy would produce the same result quickly enough.
options.misconception: treats speed as the governing criterion

options.text: The writ is issued only for a ministerial duty, a clear right, and the absence of another adequate remedy.

questions.explanation: The writ is available only where a ministerial duty is involved, the petitioner's right is clear and undeniable, and no other adequate remedy exists. Error, delay, and convenience do not substitute for those elements.
questions.hint: Three elements, all of them required.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish habeas corpus from an ordinary civil appeal
questions.stem: Against the backdrop of a pending claim, the team asks the agent to distinguish the writ's use from an ordinary civil appeal.

answer.exemplar: Habeas is a collateral challenge to the fact or legality of custody, brought while the petitioner is detained or under a sentence, and it is not a second trial on the conviction or an appeal from the judgment itself. Its remedies are release, a new trial, or a new hearing, and the petitioner's failure to raise a claim in the state courts usually bars it.

questions.explanation: Habeas does not run to the conviction in the first instance and is not an appeal of the criminal judgment. It is a collateral attack on custody with non-monetary remedies, and unraised claims are usually barred.
questions.hint: Collateral challenge, not a direct appeal.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the decision rules for a motion for summary judgment

stimulus.body: A guide for new litigators states that on a motion for summary judgment the court may not weigh evidence, may not judge the credibility of witnesses, and must resolve any doubt or reasonable inference in favor of the party opposing the motion.

questions.stem: The guide supports which statement about the motion for summary judgment.

options.text: The court decides on the papers, and the party opposing the motion receives the benefit of any doubt.
The court decides on the papers, and the party moving receives the benefit of any doubt.
options.misconception: gives the doubt to the moving party

options.text: The court holds a hearing, and the party opposing the motion must prove its claims fully.
options.misconception: moves the burden to the non-moving party

options.text: The court decides only if the parties agree, since it may not rule on its own motion.
options.misconception: requires party agreement to decide the motion

questions.explanation: The motion is decided on the papers, with credibility and weighing of evidence off limits, and any doubt or reasonable inference going to the non-moving party. The court may rule without a hearing and without the parties' agreement.
questions.hint: Read the guide for who receives the doubt.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Determine which authority prevails when a decree conflicts with a later statute

stimulus.body: A consent decree entered in a federal case directs a company to collect a fee that a later federal statute says may not be charged. The company argues that the statute must be obeyed because the decree was entered before the statute took effect.

questions.stem: The scenario turns on which proposition about the two authorities.

options.text: The decree governs, because an existing judgment cannot be disturbed by later legislation.
options.misconception: makes judgments immune to later laws

options.text: The statute governs, because a decree entered earlier has no continuing force at all.
options.misconception: denies any continuing force to a decree

options.text: The statute governs the parties' rights, and the decree is reviewed as error to the extent it conflicts.
The statute governs only prospectively, so the decree is fully effective for past charges.
options.misconception: makes the statute purely prospective here

questions.explanation: The statute sets the parties' rights, and a decree that conflicts with it is reviewed as error to the extent of the conflict. Entry earlier does not make a judgment immune to a later law, nor does it nullify the judgment.
questions.hint: Later law governs the rights; earlier order faces review.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Sequence statutory and constitutional issues and identify who may raise them
questions.stem: Inside the platform group, the recurring question now has two stages: which issue first, and who may raise it.

options.text: Statutory first if it can resolve the case; constitutional only if a party with standing must raise it.
Constitutional first in every case; any member of the public may raise the constitutional issue.
options.misconception: makes constitutional priority universal and standing free

options.text: Statutory first only if the court prefers; constitutional issues may be raised by the court itself.
options.misconception: lets preference and judicial self-help govern

options.text: Constitutional first if the statute is unclear; the issue may be raised by any non-party.
options.misconception: invents non-party standing and a clarity trigger

questions.explanation: A court resolves the case on the statute when it can and reaches the constitutional issue only if it must, and only a party who may raise it can present it. Neither the court's preference nor any non-party can add the issue.
questions.hint: Necessity decides the order, standing decides the raiser.

questions.learningObjective: State the outer limit of relief a court may award
questions.stem: Quite apart from policy, the team asks what the court may not do when the record supports less relief than a party requested.

options.text: It may not award partial relief, because a judgment must grant the entire claim or none of it.
options.misconception: believes partial relief is unavailable

options.text: It may award the full amount requested, because requests set the outer limit of relief.
options.misconception: makes the request the ceiling of relief

options.text: It may award nothing at all, because partial relief is not a form of judgment.
options.misconception: denies that partial relief is available

options.text: It may award less than requested but supported relief, since the proof fixes the outer limit.

questions.explanation: The proof, not the request, fixes the outer limit of relief, and a court may award less than was asked for. Partial relief is a normal judgment, and the court's discretion is bounded by the record rather than by the demand.
questions.hint: The record sets the ceiling, not the demand.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a consent decree with a private settlement
questions.stem: Because a partner asked, the agent explains how a consent decree compares with a settlement that is never entered by the court.

answer.exemplar: A private settlement is a contract between the parties and is enforceable only by a breach-of-contract action. A consent decree is the same negotiated agreement entered by a court as a judgment, so it becomes an order of the court and is enforceable by contempt. It binds the parties rather than establishing any rule for others.

questions.explanation: The difference lies in the court's entry of the agreement as a judgment, which makes it enforceable by contempt rather than by a contract suit. The binding effect remains limited to the parties in either case.
questions.hint: Court entry is what changes the enforcement route.

questions.learningObjective: Read an appellate disposition for what it decided and left open

options.misconception: misreads the panel's disposition of the statute

questions.explanation: The panel reversed the statutory error, declined to reach the alternative constitutional argument, and remanded. It neither entered judgment for the losing party nor decided the reserved question.
questions.hint: Separate what was decided from what was reserved.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the discretionary-duty limit to a writ of mandamus

stimulus.body: A licensing board must act on a completed application within sixty days but retains discretion over the terms of any license it grants. An applicant asks a court to compel the board to issue a license with specific terms the applicant prefers.

questions.stem: The writ the applicant seeks runs into which obstacle.

options.text: The obstacle is that no court may entertain a petition from an applicant at all.
options.misconception: denies standing to applicants generally

options.text: The obstacle is that the board's deadline is long past, so the writ is barred by delay.
options.misconception: makes delay the only bar to the writ

options.text: The obstacle is that terms of the license are discretionary, and the writ reaches ministerial duties only.
The obstacle is that a license application must first be refused before a court may act.
options.misconception: invents a prior-refusal requirement

questions.explanation: Because the terms of the license are discretionary, the duty the applicant wants compelled is not ministerial, and the writ does not reach it. Delay and prior refusal are not the obstacles.
questions.hint: Look for the part the official still gets to choose.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how habeas relates to the underlying criminal trial
questions.stem: Behind the feature request, the legal question is how a habeas petition and the underlying trial relate.

options.text: The petition challenges custody and must exhaust state remedies; the trial remains valid unless vacated.
The petition reopens the trial automatically; the trial is set aside once the petition is filed.
options.misconception: treats filing as vacating the conviction

options.text: The petition replaces the trial; the state need not be heard because the claim was already decided.
options.misconception: collapses habeas into the original proceeding

options.text: The petition cannot proceed at all once the sentence has been fully served.
options.misconception: assumes completion of a sentence ends custody

questions.explanation: Habeas is a collateral challenge to custody that does not disturb the conviction directly, and the petitioner must exhaust state remedies first. Filing a petition neither vacates the trial nor removes the state from the case.
questions.hint: Collateral means it runs alongside, not through, the trial.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State when judgment may be entered for the non-moving party
questions.stem: Under the revised policy, the team asks when the court may enter judgment for the party who did not move.

options.text: Whenever the court believes that party's evidence is stronger, because judgment ends the dispute.
options.misconception: substitutes belief for the legal standard

options.text: When the moving party fails to show the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact.
Whenever the opposing party has not filed a response within the court's deadline.
options.misconception: treats default as proof of no dispute

options.text: Only when the moving party's motion was unopposed, because consent makes judgment certain.
options.misconception: requires an unopposed motion for judgment

questions.explanation: A court may enter judgment for the non-moving party only where the movant has failed to show the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact. Belief, default, and the absence of opposition do not substitute.
questions.hint: The movant must fail on the legal test, not merely seem weak.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court order that conflicts with a statute
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a statutory amendment on an existing order
questions.stem: Whatever the outcome, the agent is asked to describe what a court should do when a statute is amended after the order was entered.

answer.exemplar: The court should apply the amended statute to the order, because a statute operates prospectively and the parties' rights are measured by the law in force at the time the new action is taken. If the amendment makes the earlier order inconsistent with the governing law, the inconsistency becomes an error of law that the reviewing court may correct.

questions.explanation: Rights are measured by the law in force when the new action is taken, so an amendment governs the next step. An order that conflicts with the amended statute becomes reviewable error rather than a protected final result.
questions.hint: New law governs the next step in the litigation.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify how an appellate panel may leave a constitutional question undecided

stimulus.body: An opinion states that the panel had no occasion to reach the question whether the statute's breadth satisfied the constitution, because a narrower construction was available and made the case resolvable on the statute alone.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, the panel's approach to the constitutional question was which of the following.

options.text: It decided the constitutional question first, because constitutional doubts outrank any construction.
options.misconception: makes constitutional priority automatic

options.text: It avoided the statutory question by ruling on the constitutional issue alone.
options.misconception: reverses the order of decision

options.text: It declined the case because the constitutional question could not be answered.
options.misconception: makes a reserved question a ground for dismissal

options.text: It left the constitutional question undecided and resolved the case on the statute instead.

questions.explanation: The panel had no occasion to reach the constitutional question because a narrower construction resolved the case on the statute alone. Avoiding a constitutional issue is the ordinary practice, not an evasion of duty.
questions.hint: No occasion to reach it means no need to decide it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether a declaration is confined to the controversy decided

stimulus.body: A trade group sues a regulator and asks the court to declare that every future permit the regulator issues is unlawful. The court grants the group's request for a declaration limited to the permit that was actually denied to one of the group's members.

questions.stem: The scope of the declaration described in the scenario is best understood how.

options.text: As invalid, because a court must address all permits once one has been declared unlawful.
options.misconception: requires a court to speak to future permits

options.text: As properly confined, because the court addressed the controversy and the member actually injured.
As void, because a declaration aimed at a class of permits cannot be made at all.
options.misconception: treats any group-wide declaration as void

options.text: As excessive, because a declaration is always limited to the parties in the courtroom.
options.misconception: forgets that members of a group may be parties

questions.explanation: The declaration is confined to the controversy and the member actually injured, which is what the court may decide. A court may speak for a properly represented group, so the category is not void.
questions.hint: Confine the ruling to the controversy and the injury.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: State the subject and binding effect of a consent decree
questions.stem: Yet the appeal continues, so the team asks two things about the settlement now on appeal: what it covers, and what it binds.

options.text: It covers the claims the parties settled and binds the parties and their successors in interest.
It covers every claim the plaintiffs could have raised and binds every similarly situated company.
options.misconception: expands both the subject and the binding effect

options.text: It covers only the payment terms and binds nobody, because it was never signed.
options.misconception: confuses a settlement with a signed contract

options.text: It covers the claims the parties settled and binds the court that entered it forever.
options.misconception: makes the decree bind the court

questions.explanation: A consent decree covers the claims the parties actually settled and binds the parties and their successors in interest. It neither sweeps in unsettled claims nor binds anyone who was not a party.
questions.hint: Scope and binding effect are two separate questions.
